abstract
Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is an autoimmune neurological disorder characterized by stiffness of the
skeletal muscle with superimposed spasms and production of autoantibodies to glutamic acid decarbox-
ylase (GAD) and amphiphysin. The disorder results from B cell-mediated clonal production of autoanti-
bodies, requiring treatment with immunosuppressors; however, treatment results have been
somewhat inconsistent. We report the results of rituximab treatment in a patient with SPS associated
with a thymoma, diabetes mellitus, autoimmune thyroiditis and the presence of anti-GAD and anti-
amphiphysin autoantibodies. The patient experienced a partial improvement following a thymectomy
and the administration of prednisone, intravenous immunoglobulins and mycophenolate mofetil. Treat-
ment with rituximab was followed by a complete sustained remission and the disappearance of serum
anti-amphiphysin antibodies.

2. Case report
A 53-year-old caucasian man was admitted to our unit for pain-
ful muscle spasms affecting the neck, back, arms and legs and a
stiffness of the spinal column, and muscles of the abdomen and
legs. The patient was bed-bound. His muscle tone was markedly
increased in all muscle groups, predominantly in the axial and
proximal limb muscles, and his leg spasms were precipitated by
movement, startle, and light touch. The spinal column was hyper-
lordotic, and the patient was unable to walk. In a standing position,
the maximum hand–ground distance was 60 cm. Electromyogra-
phy studies demonstrated spontaneous involuntary motor unit
potentials affecting both the agonist and antagonist muscles.
Serum anti-GAD antibodies were positive and had a titre of
90 IU/mL (N < 1.5); anti-amphiphysin antibodies were also positive
and had a titre of more than 1/6400 IU/mL. The patient carried the
allele DQB1 06. Anti-Hu, Yo, RI, CV2, MA1 and MA2 antibodies
were negative. Tomodensitometry and a positron emission tomog-
raphy (PET)/CT scan showed a thymoma and a histological exami-
nation revealed it was a lympho-epithelial type. Surgical resection
was followed by treatment with prednisone, 60 mg/day, for

1 month. This was progressively reduced to 10 mg/day for
28 months, and administered with 400 mg/day of i.v. Ig for 5 days,
which was repeated monthly for 14 months. In addition, 1 g MM
was given twice daily with 20 mg/day diazepam and 30 mg/day
baclofen; the patient also underwent intensive physiotherapy.
His condition improved gradually yet he experienced resid-
ual stiffness mainly affecting the back, and muscles of the abdo-
men and limbs; however, the spasms were suppressed. The
patient was able to walk, but his gait was slow and awkward.
The anti-amphiphysin antibody titre fell to 1/1600 IU/mL, but
anti-GAD antibodies remained elevated with a titre ranging
between 70.74 IU/mL and 142.7 IU/mL. The patient developed dia-
betes mellitus 6 months after diagnosis as well as autoimmune
thyroiditis and had an anti-thyroperoxidase antibody titre of
1/800 IU/mL.
One year after a thymectomy, while the patient was still being
treated with prednisone, monthly i.v. Ig and MM, his muscle pains
and stiffness worsened and spasms reappeared in his legs. Conse-
quently, diazepam and baclofen were increased to 30 mg/day and
40 mg/day, respectively, without success. Rituximab was adminis-
tered i.v. at a dose of 350 mg/m
2 per week, for 4 weeks. After
15 days, contraction of the spinal muscles showed improvement
and the hand–ground distance was 30 cm. The abdominal stiffness
had disappeared, and the patient was able to walk a distance of
more than 500 metres, as well as stand and shower himself. Diaz-
epam and baclofen were tapered to 5 mg/day and 10 mg/day,
respectively, without relapse. The anti-amphiphysin antibody titre
fell from 1/1600 IU/mL to 1/100 IU/mL.
The patient’s symptoms began to reappear 8 months later and
he was given a single dose of rituximab. His condition improved
again after 8 days and his pain and muscle stiffness completely dis-
appeared with a total recovery of independence. Anti-amphiphysin
antibodies were no longer detectable. Twenty months after the
second administration of rituximab the patient’s condition re-
mained stable. He was able to walk and run normally, drive a
car, and was able to work. While the serum anti-amphiphysin anti-
bodies were no longer detectable, anti-GAD antibodies remained
strongly positive (Table 1). Nevertheless, his diabetes mellitus im-
proved, as conﬁrmed by a reduction of antidiabetic drugs, and no
hypothyroidism was detected during follow-up. Tomodensitome-
try was repeated every 6 months for 2 years, and was completed
by a PET/CT scan 1 year after the diagnosis, which did not show
any tumor aside from the thymoma.
